evidence_records.Authors: Awais Hameed Khan; Hiruni Kegalle; Rhea D'Silva; Ned Watt; Daniel Whelan-Shamy; Lida Ghahremanlou; Liam Magee
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: journal publication; peer-review status not independently verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Official arXiv record submitted 11 May 2024 and lists the journal reference Microsoft Journal for Applied Research, volume 21, pages 69–87.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: two-stage Robodebt pilot using updated model/prompt confirmation
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare human and LLM theme assignments on controversial Robodebt statements and use discrepancies to develop reflexive prompt-design guidance.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke; deliberative consensus coding
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-4 first induces an eleven-theme closed codebook, two human authors and two LLMs independently assign themes to seventeen hand-selected statements, thresholded matrices are compared, and a second prompt/model experiment probes alignment sensitivity.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: LLM-assisted inductive codebook generation followed by deductive theme assignment
evidence_records.Domain: Australian politics, welfare policy, and controversial public discourse
evidence_records.Dataset name: Robodebt statements from #NotMyDebt and a parliamentary/Hansard speech
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public online advocacy and government transcript sources
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 17 statements × 11 themes (187 statement-theme decisions per coder)
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public statements about a harmful welfare-debt controversy; victims' statements may remain socially sensitive
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT-4; Meta Llama 2; confirmation experiment with Claude 3 Opus and Llama 3
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4 June 2023; Llama 2 February 2023; GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, and Llama 3 April 2024 releases; parameter sizes/snapshots not fully reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Collaboratively refined role/context prompt with 0–100 theme relevance scores, temperature 0.1, 50% and 70% thresholds, followed by revised skeptical/stepwise prompts; the main system prompt is printed.
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: parallel single-model coders rather than a communicating multi-agent system
evidence_records.Agent roles: GPT-4 and Llama 2 act as independent machine coders; humans act as independent coders then deliberate to consensus.
evidence_records.Human role: Two author-researchers curate statements, review/refine the LLM-generated codebook, independently code, deliberate disagreements, redesign prompts, and interpret model-human differences.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: statement-theme pair
evidence_records.Generated outputs: eleven-theme codebook, probability-weighted theme assignments, dichotomized coder matrices, comparisons, and a 58-card AI Sub Zero Bias toolkit
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Every coder decision is associated with one of seventeen listed source statements, although free-form rationales are not systematically evaluated.
evidence_records.Baselines: two human coders/consensus and cross-model GPT-4 versus Llama 2 comparisons; later GPT-4/Claude 3/Llama 3 prompt confirmation
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one principal run per model/prompt plus a later revised-prompt/model experiment; stochastic replicates not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: agreement counts/percentages and theme-level, statement-level, and pairwise correlations at 50% and 70% thresholds
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two author coders independently assign themes, deliberate to consensus, and qualitatively inspect disagreements with models.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two multidisciplinary author-researchers; external independent evaluators not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Human-machine and machine-machine agreement/correlation are reported; pre-consensus human-human reliability is not reported.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive agreement and correlations under two post-hoc thresholds; uncertainty tests are not reported
evidence_records.Principal results: Agreement varies by model and threshold, model pairs sometimes agree more with each other than with humans, prompt instructions can move models toward human judgments, and disagreements expose biases on both sides rather than a single gold interpretation.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: The article argues that verification and prompt iteration may add labor; monetary cost and wall-clock comparisons are not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The paper discusses political bias, sensitive-data transmission, de-identification effects, black-box accountability, and risks of bypassing human review; formal ethics approval is not reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Main prompt, all seventeen statements, result matrices, threshold rules, and card toolkit are reported; complete code/API logs and exact snapshots are not reported.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Small selective corpus, curator/coder bias, GPT-generated initial themes, prompt sensitivity, threshold degrees of freedom, model updates, and absence of generalizability.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Theme thresholds are researcher-chosen, codebook induction and evaluation reuse GPT-4, and public-source identities/political stance may cue assignments.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Extends earlier LLM thematic-analysis work with a deliberately controversial corpus and explicit human/model plurality; its second experiment is dependent confirmation, not a separate study.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Materially supports evaluation without a singular ground truth and shows why threshold, prompt, model, and political-framing perturbations must be reported.

evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none

evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: none

evidence_records.Domain: data-science education and software-engineering Scrum practice
evidence_records.Dataset name: Teaching Data Science at UCSB interviews; Alami Scrum interview dataset (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.6624064)
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: open interview datasets
evidence_records.Number of participants: 49 interview records; whether records equal unique participants is not explicitly verified
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 135 generated codes/53 unique for teaching; 534 generated codes/66 unique for Scrum
evidence_records.Document length: whole interviews processed with a 16k-token model; lengths not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: open interview data; privacy/de-identification details are inherited from source datasets and not re-audited
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT3.5-Turbo-16k; snapshot not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Prompt 1 requests up to fifteen named/described codes with a participant quote in JSON; Prompt 2 asks true/false semantic-duplicate judgments against the growing codebook; temperature 0.
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers design prompts, order interviews, calculate metrics, and interpret curves; no human validates individual duplicate judgments or code quality.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: whole interview for code generation and individual generated code for duplicate checking
evidence_records.Generated outputs: quote-bearing initial codes, cumulative and cumulative-unique codebooks, saturation curves, slope-ratio metric, and a code-similarity matrix
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Each generated code must include a source participant quote, although quote correctness is not independently evaluated.
evidence_records.Baselines: two datasets with different sizes/structure; no human saturation estimate or alternative deduplication baseline
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one interview order/run per dataset; no seeds or stochastic replicates
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: unique/total code ratio proposed as ITS slope ratio (0.39 teaching; 0.12 Scrum) and all-mpnet-base-v2 cosine similarity among Scrum unique codes
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: none
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive cumulative curves, ratios, a conceptual probability model, and embedding similarity; no validation against human judgments
evidence_records.Principal results: Unique codebooks grow more slowly than total codebooks, yielding ratios of 0.39 and 0.12; the authors treat the metric as a working hypothesis and note that dataset structure, code-space size, and order may drive it.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k is selected partly for lower cost; actual token counts, cost, and time are not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Use of open data is reported; ethics, consent, de-identification, and API retention are not discussed in detail.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Both prompts, formulas, codebook counts, figures, model/temperature, and one dataset DOI are reported; code and generated codebooks are not linked.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Metric validity remains untested; dataset structure affects results; interview order may change saturation; a posteriori versus sequential reduction and larger code spaces require study.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The same LLM generates and adjudicates code duplicates, the metric can reward generic/repetitive coding, embedding distinctness is not interpretive validity, and no human reference validates code quality.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Extends De Paoli's earlier GPT-3.5 thematic-analysis procedure and reuses its teaching dataset; not an independent replication of that family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A key candidate metric whose unvalidated construct and generator-evaluator circularity motivate independent, plurality-aware, order-sensitive metric validation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Dunivin, Z. O. (2024). Scalable Qualitative Coding with LLMs: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Matches Human Performance in Some Hermeneutic Tasks. arXiv:2401.15170v2. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2401.15170
evidence_records.Title: Scalable Qualitative Coding with LLMs: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Matches Human Performance in Some Hermeneutic Tasks
evidence_records.Authors: Zackary Okun Dunivin
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 26 January 2024 and v2 submitted 12 February 2024; the official record reports no journal reference or publisher DOI.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: standalone Du Bois/New York Times deductive-coding study
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 can apply a difficult socio-historical codebook and identify prompt/codebook practices that improve agreement with human coding.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: qualitative coding/content analysis of hermeneutic socio-historical categories
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Nine binary codes are adapted iteratively for LLM use, applied zero-shot to paragraph passages under per-code versus full-codebook and rationale versus no-rationale conditions, and compared with a withheld human-derived label set.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: deductive application of a human-developed codebook
evidence_records.Domain: digital humanities and historical sociology; representations of W.E.B. Du Bois in news
evidence_records.Dataset name: New York Times W.E.B. Du Bois passage corpus
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public research package on OSF; underlying news articles may remain subject to publisher copyright
evidence_records.Number of documents: 232 automatically extracted paragraph passages; 111 gold-standard passages used in the reported agreement table
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 232 passages mentioning W.E.B. Du Bois from New York Times articles dated 1970–2023
evidence_records.Document length: mean 94 words (SD 70) and 3.75 sentences (SD 2.88) per passage
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: historical public-news material; no participant data are reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 API models; exact snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Zero-shot system/user prompts with role, code definition, optional justification/rationale, and machine-readable decision; per-code and full-codebook variants are compared.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no model fine-tuning; the human codebook was iteratively rewritten for LLM interpretation
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers developed and refined the codebook, created the hidden gold standard, inspected rationales and errors, and retained responsibility for deciding whether automation was suitable.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: paragraph-length news passage
evidence_records.Generated outputs: binary code assignments and, in chain-of-thought conditions, textual rationales
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Each prediction is tied to a source passage and its generated rationale, but rationale faithfulness is not independently established.
evidence_records.Baselines: withheld human-derived gold-standard labels; GPT-3.5; per-code versus full-codebook prompts; rationale versus no-rationale prompts
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: not reported; temperature 0 and top_p 1 are reported, but repeated stochastic runs are not
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa for each of nine codes and mean kappa across codes
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Agreement is computed against a human-derived gold standard hidden during LLM development; no separate blind qualitative-output panel is reported.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: human codebook developers, including the author and a named collaborator; exact coder count and training protocol are not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: GPT-4 per-code with rationale mean kappa 0.68; 8/9 codes at or above 0.60 and 3/9 at or above 0.79; GPT-3.5 mean kappa 0.34
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive comparison of per-code Cohen's kappa across six model/prompt configurations
evidence_records.Principal results: GPT-4 substantially outperformed GPT-3.5; per-code prompting and requested rationales generally improved agreement, while one implicit activist-voice code remained poor (best kappa 0.34).
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: No formal ethics or privacy protocol is reported; the empirical corpus is public historical news rather than participant data.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Code and data are linked at https://osf.io/k4fg9; prompts and codebook examples appear in the paper; exact API snapshots are absent.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Performance varies by code and interpretive difficulty; the study covers one codebook, GPT-4 struggles with edge cases and implicit information, and the authors advise manual review for uncertain outputs.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Iterative codebook tuning risks development-set overfitting, human-gold construction is underreported, kappa cannot establish interpretive quality, and claims about future majority-codebook viability extrapolate beyond one case.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Compares directly with earlier deductive-coding studies but uses an independent Du Bois/news corpus and codebook.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Direct RQ evidence that prompt granularity and requested rationales affect agreement, while also motivating held-out evaluation, rationale-faithfulness checks, and code-level failure analysis.

evidence_records.Authors: Stefano De Paoli
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 12 April 2024; the official record reports no journal reference or publisher DOI.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: De Paoli inductive-TA procedure family; reuses the author's earlier staged prompting procedure but a new Italian dataset
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether a staged LLM-supported inductive thematic analysis can operate directly on Italian interviews and produce themes resembling an earlier human analysis.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive thematic analysis following phases 2–4 of Braun and Clarke
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-3.5-Turbo generates quote-bearing initial codes per interview; GPT-4-Turbo groups all codes into at least nine themes and varies temperature for refinement; outputs are manually paired with Grounded Theory categories and evaluated by embeddings and one source-study author.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive generation with a human-analysis comparator
evidence_records.Domain: arts and humanities scholars' concepts and uses of data
evidence_records.Dataset name: What do we mean by 'data' in the arts and humanities? interview transcripts
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public Zenodo dataset, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.6123290
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 185 LLM-generated initial codes (about 10 per interview); source word count not reported
evidence_records.Language: Italian; one interview also tested with an English prompt while retaining Italian outputs
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public research interviews; the paper does not re-audit consent or de-identification for cloud processing
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-3.5-Turbo for initial coding and GPT-4-Turbo for themes; snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Zero-shot Italian prompts request code names, descriptions and representative quotations, then at least nine themes; one English-prompt comparison and three temperature-based theme refinements are run.
evidence_records.Human role: The author selected data, designed prompts, manually paired themes to prior categories, adjusted category wording for comparison, and interpreted results; one original-study author rated the paired themes.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: interview transcript for initial coding and aggregate code list for theme generation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 185 initial codes with descriptions/quotes and multiple nine-theme codebooks
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Initial codes include representative source quotations; theme-level traceability is through listed underlying codes rather than complete passage links.
evidence_records.Baselines: eight high-level categories from an earlier QualCoder Grounded Theory analysis; Italian-versus-English prompt comparison
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one initial analysis plus theme-generation runs at temperatures 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75; seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Sentence-BERT cosine similarity between manually paired human-category and LLM-theme labels; code similarity for one Italian-versus-English prompt test
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: The lead author of the original dataset analysis scored how well six paired LLM themes captured human-category meaning on a 0–10 scale.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one original-study lead author familiar with the dataset and human analysis
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive cosine similarities and six single-rater scores; no inferential testing
evidence_records.Principal results: The model produced 185 codes and nine themes; six of seven manually paired label comparisons exceeded cosine 0.60, one was 0.43 before wording adjustment, one human category was missed, and the original analyst rated the six displayed pairs 8–10/10.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: GPT-3.5-Turbo is described as relatively inexpensive, but measured time and monetary cost are not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Open-data use is reported; participant consent, cloud-processing safeguards, and a new ethics determination are not reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: The source transcripts and human QualCoder file are public on Zenodo and prompt wording is shown; analysis scripts, full outputs, and exact model snapshots are not linked.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Only Italian and one dataset are tested; findings apply only where a language is supported, and further language/model tests are required.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Grounded Theory categories are treated as a thematic-analysis comparator, pairs and wording were selected by the same author, label embeddings do not validate interpretations, and the human evaluation has one nonblind rater.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Extends De Paoli's 2023 inductive-TA workflow to Italian and is methodologically dependent on that procedure, but uses Gualandi et al.'s separate dataset and human analysis.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Adds rare multilingual evidence and exposes the need for cross-language, native-speaker, source-grounded, and plurality-aware evaluation rather than translated-label similarity alone.

evidence_records.Authors: He Zhang; Chuhao Wu; Jingyi Xie; Fiona Rubino; Sydney Graver; ChanMin Kim; John M. Carroll; Jie Cai
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 20 July 2024; the official record flags substantial text overlap with arXiv:2310.07061 and reports no peer-reviewed venue.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: QualiGPT family; substantial-overlap successor to arXiv:2310.07061, which is not an independent study
evidence_records.Research objective: Design QualiGPT as an accessible API-based qualitative-coding tool and compare its inductive and deductive outputs with human coding on simulated and real data.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive and deductive qualitative coding/thematic analysis
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: A prompt-template interface chunks uploaded text, returns themes/descriptions/quotes/counts, and is evaluated through one synthetic efficiency case plus inductive and deductive code-assignment comparisons on Discord messages.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: both inductive and deductive
evidence_records.Domain: online developer community and simulated remote-work focus group
evidence_records.Dataset name: simulated remote-work focus group and public TwitchDev Discord-message sample
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: simulated test data are provided; the real sample is drawn from a public Discord server, but the full analyzed dataset release status is not reported
evidence_records.Number of documents: synthetic focus-group file plus 200 real entries for inductive coding and another 200 for deductive coding
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: synthetic dataset reported as 9,309 words; 400 real Discord entries across the two coding cases
evidence_records.Document length: real entries are individual messages; synthetic response lengths are reported heterogeneously and cannot be reconciled into a single reliable mean
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public community messages were stripped of labels; identifiable-information screening and participant consent are not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5; API snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Customizable templates combine task background, description, processing method, output schema, role prompting and acknowledgement/context prompts; a 50-example prior-knowledge condition is also tested.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: none; prompts and a human-refined 54-label codebook provide task adaptation
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single-model calls through a single-user tool
evidence_records.Human role: Two research assistants independently code real data and negotiate inductive labels; a senior researcher helps refine the codebook; users control prompts, inspect quote-bearing outputs, and export results.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: individual Discord message or simulated focus-group response
evidence_records.Generated outputs: inductive labels; deductive labels; themes, descriptions, quotations and participant counts; CSV/text exports
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: QualiGPT outputs supporting quotations with themes and can export the prompt/data/output trail; faithfulness and quote-selection completeness are not independently tested.
evidence_records.Baselines: two human coders; ChatGPT web workflow; GPT-4, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 across conditions
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: three timed synthetic analyses and three independent GPT-4 deductive-coding rounds; seeds and sampling parameters not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa and Fleiss' kappa
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Human/LLM labels are manually judged semantically equivalent for inductive kappa; deductive kappa compares two research assistants and multiple model outputs.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two research assistants and one senior researcher; exact qualitative experience is not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: inductive human-versus-GPT-4 kappa 0.57; human-human deductive kappa 0.73; human-plus-GPT-4 Fleiss kappa 0.44–0.50; GPT-4 repeated-run kappa 0.87; GPT-4o 0.38 and Claude 3.5 0.42 with humans
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive kappa comparisons; no inferential tests
evidence_records.Principal results: QualiGPT completed the synthetic workflow in a mean 96.5 seconds; model-human agreement was moderate and below human-human agreement, while repeated GPT-4 outputs agreed strongly with one another.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Three synthetic runs averaged 96.5 seconds; manual inductive coding of 200 entries took several hours plus nearly one week of discussion; monetary cost is not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The design uses user-supplied API keys and claims session deletion/API privacy advantages, but no ethics review, consent, retention audit, or security evaluation is reported for public Discord data.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Synthetic data and many prompt examples are supplied; the paper cites a QualiGPT tool record, but full real data, exact snapshots, complete source code, and run logs are not reported as available.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: The discussion notes model inconsistency, context limits, prompt sensitivity, privacy, hallucinations, and the continuing need for human negotiation and reflective coding.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The inductive agreement label is itself a post-hoc subjective binary judgment, data partitions are small and underdescribed, kappa is treated as quality evidence, and tool-benefit claims exceed the measured usability evidence.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Expanded publication-family version of the earlier QualiGPT preprint arXiv:2310.07061; it should be counted once, not as an independent replication.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Provides direct workflow, efficiency and stability evidence while motivating independent semantic adjudication, transparent family handling, and evaluation beyond inter-rater agreement.

evidence_records.Venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education

evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: arXiv 2309.17447 / 2024 journal version family; count once
evidence_records.Research objective: Evaluate zero-shot GPT workflows for classification, extraction, inductive thematic analysis and sentiment analysis of educational survey feedback.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive and deductive thematic analysis embedded in composable survey-analysis workflows
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT derives batch-level themes, classifies comments into themes, coalesces themes, and performs related fixed-label/extraction/sentiment tasks; most quantitative validation concerns component classification rather than the inductive themes themselves.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid
evidence_records.Domain: online biomedical-science course feedback
evidence_records.Dataset name: Harvard Medical School HMX end-of-course survey responses
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted; data may be requested subject to university ethics-board approval
evidence_records.Number of documents: 2,500 evaluation responses (625 per question) plus 2,000 development comments, sampled from 50,525 total responses
evidence_records.Number of participants: not reported; learners answered about two of four questions on average
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 2,500 evaluation comments across 365 course iterations and 15 courses
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: private student and teacher feedback; locally screened for names and not released to protect anonymity
evidence_records.Exact model/version: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and GPT-4-0314 for multilabel classification; gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 and GPT-4-0613 for other tasks

evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single-model calls composed into multi-step workflows
evidence_records.Human role: Four authors develop/refine labels and annotate data; humans inspect reasoning, tune prompts, supply task ground truth, and retain responsibility for educational use.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: individual open-ended survey comment or extracted comment span
evidence_records.Generated outputs: themes, structured labels, extracted quotations, sentiment labels and chain-of-thought text
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Extraction preserves exact excerpts and outputs structured reasoning, but the paper acknowledges that chain-of-thought may be post-hoc and theme-to-source traceability is batch based.
evidence_records.Baselines: four expert human annotators, SetFit classifier and Twitter-RoBERTa sentiment classifier; GPT-3.5 versus GPT-4
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one principal evaluation per task/model at temperature 0; automatic retries are reported, but repeated independent runs/seeds are not
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Jaccard similarity, average/macro/micro precision-recall-F1, Hamming loss, subset accuracy, binary accuracy, and a custom GPT-4 extraction rubric
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Four expert annotators provide multilabel ground truth; one expert labels binary/sentiment tasks; humans inspect extraction hallucinations and hundreds of reasoning outputs; inductive themes receive visual inspection only.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: four study authors familiar with the educational program; one serves as expert annotator for some component tasks
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: human-human mean Jaccard 81.24%; mean across human/GPT-4 pairs 80.60%; 57% of 2,500 rows have unanimous four-human label agreement
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive performance metrics; no inferential comparison of models is reported
evidence_records.Principal results: GPT-4 substantially outperformed GPT-3.5 and matched human pairwise Jaccard on multilabel coding; GPT-4 consensus-row macro F1 was 89.78, binary F1 95.79 and sentiment macro F1 80.78, while inductive-theme quality lacked a validated metric.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: About $300 total API cost including prompt tuning; GPT-4 handled 100 comments in about 10 seconds for most tasks and about one minute for extraction evaluation; per-100-comment task prices are reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Harvard determined the study was not human-subjects research; comments were screened for names, withheld from open release, and access requires ethics-board approval.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Prompts and function schemas are in electronic supplements; data are restricted; code and executable run package are not reported.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: One English biomedical-education domain, high prompt dependence, limited model families, and behavior that may change with model updates.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Theme quality is inferred largely from downstream fixed-label performance, the custom extraction evaluator uses GPT-4 to assess GPT outputs, and inspecting rationale does not establish faithful internal reasoning.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: The 2023 arXiv and 2024 journal article are the same publication family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A strong large-corpus efficiency/component benchmark, but also a clear example of why thematic validity, evaluator independence, rationale faithfulness, privacy, and task-level error propagation need separate assessment.

evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Foundational RQ evidence for staged inductive workflows, prompt/temperature sensitivity and quote grounding, while sharply motivating blind comparison, plurality-aware evaluation, and consent/privacy safeguards.

evidence_records.Research objective: Compare ChatGPT-4 with the rule-based Etuma tool for keyword/topic classification in Finnish qualitative content analysis and assess reproducibility, transparency and research integrity.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: qualitative content analysis combining distant and close reading
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: The same Finnish texts are classified zero-shot by a custom ChatGPT-4 bot and Etuma; the sole author close-reads and validates a random 20-text subset, then compares precision, recall, F1, granularity and scientific-principle compliance.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive topic/keyword discovery with human validation and later refinement
evidence_records.Domain: Finnish political energy discourse and electric-car subsidies
evidence_records.Dataset name: subset of a Finnish energy-discourse corpus from Mohawk Analytics and ParliamentSampo
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: parliamentary speeches are public; availability and redistribution status of scraped social-media comments are not reported
evidence_records.Number of documents: 73 stated documents (40 social-media comments and 33 parliamentary speeches); the reported social-source subtype counts sum to 44, an internal inconsistency
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: subset drawn from 110,295 social-media comments and 25,872 parliamentary speeches; validation uses 10 texts from each source
evidence_records.Document length: social comments 20–155 words; parliamentary speeches 72–662 words
evidence_records.Language: Finnish; examples translated to English for publication
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public political/social discourse; targeted @mentions were removed, but consent and platform-governance details are not reported
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI ChatGPT-4 via Poe.com and Etuma rule-based NLP
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT version 4 accessed in September 2023 through Poe.com; exact snapshot not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: A zero-shot custom-bot prompt at temperature 0 requests all keywords and topics; later question-refinement and few-shot-like targeted prompts are explored.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no model fine-tuning; prompt engineering for ChatGPT and manual ontology-rule refinement for Etuma
evidence_records.Human role: The sole researcher defines the topic, cleans data, close-reads material, manually establishes validation keywords, inspects hallucinations and retains final analytical judgment.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: social-media comment or parliamentary speech
evidence_records.Generated outputs: keywords and broad topic labels
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Outputs are stored alongside source texts in a spreadsheet and manually checked; ChatGPT supplies no formal source-only rationale or persistent provenance link.
evidence_records.Baselines: Etuma rule-based/supervised ontology tool and sole-author close-reading labels
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: The author repeated some identical prompts in new chats and observed differences; exact repeat count and seeds are not reported.
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: precision, recall and F1 on the 20-text human-validation sample
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: The sole author manually extracts all potentially relevant keywords in 10 random texts per source and treats these as reference labels.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one political-discourse researcher
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive precision, recall and F1; no inferential testing
evidence_records.Principal results: ChatGPT precision was 0.96 for both sources but recall was 0.61/0.58 and F1 0.75/0.72; Etuma precision was 0.70, recall 0.85/0.81 and F1 0.77/0.75. ChatGPT produced broader topics, occasional hallucinations and nonrepeatable results.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The paper discusses bias, misinformation, plagiarism, hallucination, researcher autonomy and the unsuitability of public LLM tools for sensitive data; no formal ethics review is reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Full prompts and chat examples are included in appendices; the analyzed corpus, spreadsheets, code and exact model snapshot are not released.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Narrow material focused on one political topic, one language and a small validation sample limit generalizability.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: One nonblind evaluator constructs the reference, document-count reporting is internally inconsistent, keywords are an incomplete proxy for qualitative interpretation, and platform/model behavior cannot be reproduced.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Independent Finnish dataset and comparison; no publication-family dependence identified.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Adds non-English and rule-based-comparator evidence, showing a high-precision/low-recall trade-off and why repeatability, granularity, transparency and researcher autonomy require explicit evaluation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Spinoso-Di Piano, C., Abbasgholizadeh Rahimi, S., & Cheung, J. C. K. (2023). Qualitative Code Suggestion: A Human-Centric Approach to Qualitative Coding. Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023, 14887–14909. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.findings-emnlp.993
evidence_records.Title: Qualitative Code Suggestion: A Human-Centric Approach to Qualitative Coding
evidence_records.Authors: Cesare Spinoso-Di Piano; Samira Abbasgholizadeh Rahimi; Jackie Chi Kit Cheung
evidence_records.Venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023, 14887–14909
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Published in Findings of EMNLP 2023, 6–10 December 2023; official ACL DOI and pagination verified.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: CVDQuoding/QCS benchmark family; dataset originates in a prior cardiovascular-risk interview project
evidence_records.Research objective: Formulate qualitative code suggestion as ranked assistive recommendations that respect coding sequence, rare codes and coder-specific styles, then benchmark NLP and GPT-3.5 approaches.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive qualitative coding/content analysis with human-centered code suggestions
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Models learn or retrieve previously assigned codes at each transcript-index saturation point and rank them for coder-highlighted spans; a separate novel-code classifier and a small human relevance study evaluate suggestions.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: sequential inductive codebook growth with deductive suggestion from codes observed so far
evidence_records.Domain: women's cardiovascular-disease risk and interest in AI health tools
evidence_records.Dataset name: CVDQuoding
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: paper describes the dataset as public, while also saying it is available by request because of sensitivity; code repository is public
evidence_records.Number of participants: 15 women at risk of cardiovascular disease
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 63,927 words and 1,175 coded text-span assignments
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: health interviews; IRB approval and consent are reported and access is mediated/request-based despite the paper's 'public' wording
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT-3.5-Turbo; SVM; DistilBERT; ConvBERT; BM25
evidence_records.Exact model/version: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, DistilBERT and ConvBERT variants; temperature 1 for GPT-3.5
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Zero-shot prompt lists all previously seen codes plus 'None of the above' and asks for a ranked assignment from the preceding interview question and highlighted answer span.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: SVM and encoder models are trained at each coder-specific saturation split; GPT-3.5 and BM25 are not fine-tuned
evidence_records.Human role: Two original qualitative coders create different sequential codebooks; future users identify passages and may accept/reject suggestions; two additional qualitative researchers judge sampled recommendations.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: coder-highlighted answer span plus the immediately preceding interview question
evidence_records.Generated outputs: ranked existing-code suggestions and a novel-code indicator
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Every suggestion is attached to a source span/question and coder-specific prior code history; GPT explanations are not generated.
evidence_records.Baselines: Okapi BM25, SVM, DistilBERT classifier, DistilBERT bi-/cross-encoders and ConvBERT cross-encoder
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 28 coder/saturation training splits are evaluated; random seeds or repeated GPT runs are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: MRR, soft NDCG@4 using BERTScore relevance, macro/micro F1 for novel-code detection, and human-judged precision@4
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two qualitative-research evaluators each judge the top-four suggestions for 32 sampled instances at K=10 as relevant or irrelevant; metrics are recomputed using those judgments.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two evaluators with qualitative-research experience; each is assigned one coder-specific sample
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported because evaluator samples are separate rather than redundantly rated
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive rank/F1 metrics and a reported statistically significant increase when human relevance labels replace original single-coder annotations; test details are not reported in the main text
evidence_records.Principal results: ConvBERT retrieval and GPT-3.5 are strongest across many saturation points; human judges find about three times more relevant codes than the original annotations, while no method beats BM25 on novel-code detection and coder style strongly changes scores.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: McGill Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences IRB A03-B22-21A approved data collection; participant consent and archived forms are reported, and the paper frames automation as assistance rather than replacement.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Code at https://github.com/cesare-spinoso/QCS.git; CVDQuoding is described and available through mediated access; hyperparameters and prompt template are reported.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: No applied user study of QCS impact, possible coder-agency loss, incomplete model exploration, poor rare/new-code detection and no use of broader LLM generation capabilities.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Original coder assignments are incomplete references, each human sample has only one evaluator, BERTScore-based gain is not interpretive validity, and offline rankings cannot establish effects on researcher judgment.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses interviews/annotations adapted from a prior cardiovascular-risk AI project; dependent dataset but a new QCS task and evaluation.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Directly supports researcher-controlled suggestions, coder-specific histories and plurality; it also provides unusually clear evidence that a single codebook reference understates valid alternative assignments.

evidence_records.Full citation: Kirsten, E., Buckmann, A., Mhaidli, A., & Becker, S. (2024). Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding. arXiv:2403.06607v1. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.06607
evidence_records.Title: Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding
evidence_records.Authors: Elisabeth Kirsten; Annalina Buckmann; Abraham Mhaidli; Steffen Becker
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 11 March 2024; the text identifies itself as a workshop submission and the official arXiv record reports no journal reference or publisher DOI.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: secondary coding experiment on a separate 47-participant digital-security/privacy interview study
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare human and LLM deductive coding agreement across semantic-to-latent tasks of increasing codebook/context complexity.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: qualitative data analysis/thematic coding spanning semantic and latent themes
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Two humans and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 apply human-generated multi-label codebooks to researcher-selected German interview segments in zero-, one- and three-shot conditions; Cohen's kappa is compared across three tasks.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: deductive application of human-generated codebooks
evidence_records.Domain: users' digital-security and privacy practices
evidence_records.Dataset name: 47-participant German digital-security/privacy interview study
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: not reported
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: researcher-extracted segments for three tasks; segment counts are not reported
evidence_records.Document length: mean segment lengths 118, 274 and 469 words for Tasks A, B and C
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: security/privacy interview data; confidentiality safeguards and participant consent for API processing are not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 API models; exact snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Task-specific German prompts include persona, study topic, methodology, research question, codebook and output format; zero-shot, one synthetic example and three synthetic examples are compared.
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers generate codebooks, select relevant transcript segments, create synthetic examples, reconcile human annotations and identify ethical/methodological implications.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: researcher-extracted interview segment
evidence_records.Generated outputs: zero or more fixed code tags per segment
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Predictions remain tied to source segments, but no rationale or quote-level explanation is produced.
evidence_records.Baselines: two human coders; GPT-3.5 versus GPT-4; zero-, one- and few-shot prompts across three tasks
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one run per reported model/task/prompt condition; seeds not reported; temperature 0
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: The final unified human annotations are the model comparator; human-human kappa is calculated on the 80% of annotations not used to build the codebook.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two human coders/researchers; training and independence are not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: human-human kappa 0.97/0.83/0.63 across Tasks A/B/C; GPT-4 zero-shot 0.97/0.75/0.56 and GPT-3.5 zero-shot 0.74/0.60/0.43
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive Cohen's-kappa comparison across conditions
evidence_records.Principal results: Agreement declines as segments/codebooks become longer and interpretation becomes more latent; GPT-4 exceeds GPT-3.5, and examples reduce formatting/hallucinated codes but do not consistently improve kappa.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: GPT-3.5 input tokens are stated to have cost about 60 times less than GPT-4 during the experiments; total cost/time is not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The discussion explicitly raises confidentiality, participant-data protection and researcher-subjectivity concerns, but no ethics approval, consent or API governance is reported for this dataset.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Prompt structure is supplied in an appendix; source data, annotations, code, full prompts/outputs and exact snapshots are not reported as available.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Preliminary short study, IRR cannot capture qualitative depth, task complexity factors are confounded, LLM reasoning is opaque, prompts are unstable and sensitive data pose confidentiality risks.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Task difficulty changes codebook size, segment length and latent content simultaneously; humans preselect segments, reconciled labels collapse plurality, and no repeated-run stability or qualitative error analysis is reported.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses data from a separate interview study but reports a new coding experiment; no duplicate publication identified.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong evidence that apparent LLM agreement is task-complexity dependent and that semantic-versus-latent interpretation, context size and codebook length must be crossed rather than conflated in evaluation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Islam, T., & Goldwasser, D. (2025). Discovering Latent Themes in Social Media Messaging: A Machine-in-the-Loop Approach Integrating LLMs. Proceedings of the 19th International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2025). arXiv:2403.10707.
evidence_records.Title: Discovering Latent Themes in Social Media Messaging: A Machine-in-the-Loop Approach Integrating LLMs
evidence_records.Authors: Tunazzina Islam; Dan Goldwasser
evidence_records.Venue: 19th International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2025)
evidence_records.Publication type: peer-reviewed conference paper with 2024 arXiv preprint
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: peer reviewed; official arXiv record reports ICWSM-2025 acceptance
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 15 March 2024 and v2 updated 15 July 2024; the current official arXiv record states acceptance at ICWSM-2025. A publisher DOI is not reported in the inspected record.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: 2024 arXiv / ICWSM-2025 publication family; count once; reuses two earlier Facebook-ad datasets and their seed themes
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop a scalable machine-in-the-loop pipeline that discovers, names and assigns fine-grained latent themes in climate and vaccine Facebook ads.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: computational thematic analysis/theme discovery grounded in prior domain concepts
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: K-means clusters unassigned ads; GPT-4 filters coherence, summarizes/names clusters and maps new ads in few-shot prompts; SBERT merges similar summaries, optional experts validate clusters, and iterations expand a pre-existing seed theme set.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: inductive cluster/theme discovery plus deductive mapping to existing and generated themes
evidence_records.Domain: US climate-change and COVID-19 vaccine campaign advertising
evidence_records.Dataset name: Climate Campaigns and COVID-19 Vaccine Campaigns Facebook-ad datasets
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public datasets and code repository
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 31,292 English Facebook advertisements
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public political/health advertising and aggregate impression demographics; no private participant transcripts are used
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT-4, Sentence-BERT, K-means, LDA and BERTopic
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4; exact snapshot not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Zero-shot GPT-4 prompts for cluster coherence, five-document summaries and names; four-shot climate and three-shot vaccine prompts for constrained theme assignment.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: none; existing theme definitions and demonstrations condition assignment
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single-model calls embedded in an iterative algorithmic pipeline
evidence_records.Human role: Two NLP/computational-social-science researchers validate cluster coherence and summaries in one two-hour session; researchers choose thresholds, seeds, theory mappings and interpret demographic/time patterns.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: Facebook advertisement
evidence_records.Generated outputs: coherence judgments, cluster summaries/names, theme assignments and demographic/temporal analyses
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Clusters retain their ads and summaries use five centroid-near examples; theme assignments map to source ads, although free-text summaries are not supplied with exhaustive evidence links.
evidence_records.Baselines: SBERT assignment, LDA topic models and BERTopic; pre-existing seed themes
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: two discovery iterations per dataset; K values and thresholds are reported, but random seeds and repeated stochastic GPT runs are not
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: coverage, accuracy, macro F1, Pearson correlations, SBERT cosine similarity and clustering heuristics
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two expert annotators judge cluster coherence and summary correctness; mapping quality uses human binary alignment judgments on 1,072 climate and 565 vaccine ads.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two NLP/CSS researchers (advanced graduate/faculty, one male and one female); the number of mapping annotators and overlap protocol are not separately reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: accuracy/macro F1 against human judgments and Pearson theme-theory correlations; uncertainty/significance for primary mapping metrics is not reported
evidence_records.Principal results: The iterative pipeline expands climate themes from 13 to 25 and vaccine themes from 15 to 23; GPT mapping reaches 88.15% accuracy/89.24 macro F1 for climate and 85.49%/81.74 for vaccine, outperforming SBERT assignment.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: one human validation session lasted two hours; GPT/API cost and end-to-end runtime are not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: An ethics statement, public-ad context, reproducibility claims and bias limitations are reported; the authors acknowledge that GPT-4 may inherit bias and that demographic-targeting interpretation is subjective.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Code and data at https://github.com/tunazislam/latent-themes-llms; prompt templates, thresholds and dataset counts are reported; exact GPT snapshot and seeds are absent.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Two case studies, reliance on proprietary GPT-4, unexamined LLM bias and subjective interpretation of age/gender targeting.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Themes begin from dependent prior seed labels, one LLM validates and summarizes its own clusters, threshold/model choices are researcher-set, and theme-theory correlation does not by itself establish qualitative validity.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Reuses climate/vaccine ad corpora and seed themes from the authors' earlier studies; the 2024 arXiv and ICWSM-2025 paper form one publication family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Extends RQs from transcript coding to scalable hybrid discovery and shows useful expert validation, but also motivates independent agents/evaluators, full cluster provenance and sensitivity tests for seeds, thresholds and stochastic runs.

evidence_records.Full citation: Chen, J., Lotsos, A., Zhao, L., Wang, G., Wilensky, U., Sherin, B., & Horn, M. S. (2024). Prompts Matter: Comparing ML/GAI Approaches for Generating Inductive Qualitative Coding Results. arXiv:2411.06316v1. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2411.06316
evidence_records.Title: Prompts Matter: Comparing ML/GAI Approaches for Generating Inductive Qualitative Coding Results
evidence_records.Authors: John Chen; Alexandros Lotsos; Lexie Zhao; Grace Wang; Uri Wilensky; Bruce Sherin; Michael S. Horn
evidence_records.Venue: arXiv; accepted for presentation at the AERA 2025 Annual Meeting
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: accepted at AERA 2025 according to the official arXiv record; archival peer-reviewed proceedings not verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 10 November 2024; official comment states 'Accepted by AERA 2025 Annual Meeting.' No publisher DOI or archival proceedings record is reported.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: AERA-2025/arXiv publication family; item/chunk prompts build on Barany et al. and Sinha et al. but use a new online-community slice
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare two established and two theory-informed ML/GAI prompting approaches for inductive open coding and assess groundedness, breadth and overlap.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive/open coding informed by thematic analysis and Grounded Theory
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: BERTopic-plus-LLM, chunk-level GPT-4o, item-level plan-then-code GPT-4o, and item-level verb-phrase GPT-4o generate codebooks from the same conversation; two authors manually flag groundedness and overly broad codes and compare with four independent human codebooks.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive
evidence_records.Domain: education technology; emergence of a Physics Lab online community
evidence_records.Dataset name: Physics Lab online message-group sample
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: an anonymized 127-message dataset is reproduced in the paper appendix; broader source-data access is not reported
evidence_records.Number of participants: not reported; messages involve designers and teachers
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 127 messages over the community's first two months
evidence_records.Document length: individual short chat messages; lengths not summarized
evidence_records.Language: English translation/status of original message language not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: usernames are anonymized in the appendix; consent, platform governance and model-data retention are not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4o; exact snapshot not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Zero-example role/research-context prompts compare cluster labeling, chunk codebook generation, item-level plan-then-multiple-code generation and item-level verb-phrase labels.
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: multiple independent machine-coder conditions, not an interacting agent system
evidence_records.Human role: Four humans independently open-code before LLM analysis; two are community insiders and two outsiders. Two authors independently audit generated codebooks for grounding/breadth and reconcile disagreements.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: conversation chunk or individual message, depending on condition
evidence_records.Generated outputs: four inductive codebooks containing 23, 48, 240 and 271 labels
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Item/chunk outputs are linked to input messages and the complete codebooks/examples are appended; the evaluation does not quantify exhaustive evidence coverage.
evidence_records.Baselines: BERTopic-plus-LLM; chunk-level prompt adapted from Barany et al.; four independent human codebooks
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one reported run per approach; seeds, temperature and repeat stability are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: counts of codes, manually flagged groundedness issues and overly broad codes; no validated automatic quality metric
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two authors independently inspect all four machine codebooks for groundedness and excessive breadth, reconcile differences, and compare examples with four independently generated human codebooks.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two author evaluators; four human coders include two long-term community researchers and two outsiders
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive counts and percentages only
evidence_records.Principal results: The verb-phrase item-level prompt generated 271 codes with no flagged grounding issue and more nuanced micro-actions, whereas other approaches produced 23–240 codes; every approach retained broad/overlapping labels and no machine codebook matched the combined human breadth.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: not reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Usernames are anonymized, but no ethics review, consent, API privacy or data-governance procedure is reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Original data, prompt adaptations and all four generated codebooks are included in extensive appendices; executable code, exact model snapshot and run seeds are not reported.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: One small research context, machines only imitate open-coding outputs rather than human engagement, no approach removes broad/overlapping codes, and manual exhaustive comparison is impractical.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Human-grounding judgments lack reported agreement, code-count proliferation may reward fragmentation, one run cannot distinguish prompt design from stochastic variance, and the reported 'best' condition has an inconsistent table/text broad-code count.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Replicates/adapts Barany et al.'s chunk procedure and Sinha et al.'s item coding; official arXiv record ties this preprint to AERA 2025, so it is one publication family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Direct RQ evidence that qualitative-theory choices encoded in prompts materially change granularity and grounding; supports crossed prompt tests, source links, human plurality and non-count-based quality criteria.

evidence_records.Full citation: Spitale, M., Cheong, J., & Gunes, H. (2024). Underneath the Numbers: Quantitative and Qualitative Gender Fairness in LLMs for Depression Prediction. arXiv:2406.08183v2. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2406.08183
evidence_records.Title: Underneath the Numbers: Quantitative and Qualitative Gender Fairness in LLMs for Depression Prediction
evidence_records.Authors: Micol Spitale; Jiaee Cheong; Hatice Gunes
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 12 June 2024 and v2 updated 14 June 2024; no journal reference or publisher DOI is reported.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: DAIC-WOZ/E-DAIC depression-prediction benchmark family; secondary fairness analysis
evidence_records.Research objective: Assess gender bias in LLM depression predictions and propose a qualitative fairness analysis of LLM-generated explanations alongside quantitative fairness metrics.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: six-step thematic analysis combined with Grounded Theory for qualitative fairness evaluation
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: ChatGPT, LLaMA 2 and Bard predict PHQ-8 depression scores under baseline and gender prompt variants; on 25 balanced test samples, two researchers thematically analyze ChatGPT/LLaMA self- and cross-critiques of explanation fairness.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: deductive fairness prompts plus inductive thematic interpretation
evidence_records.Domain: high-stakes mental-health/depression prediction and gender fairness
evidence_records.Dataset name: DAIC-WOZ and E-DAIC
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: benchmark access terms not reported in this paper; datasets are anonymized by their owners
evidence_records.Number of documents: 25 balanced dialogue samples for qualitative analysis; full quantitative test-set counts not reported in this paper
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: two depression-interview benchmarks; 25 samples in the qualitative subset
evidence_records.Document length: conversations chunked to 2,048 tokens with 500-token overlap when necessary
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: anonymized semi-clinical mental-health interviews; secondary-use governance and API safeguards are not reported
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI ChatGPT, Meta LLaMA 2 70B Chat and Google Bard
evidence_records.Exact model/version: gpt-3.5-turbo; LLaMA-2-70b-chat-hf; experimental Bard accessed October–December 2023
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: PHQ-8 baseline, gender-explicit and gender-implicit prediction prompts followed by self-/cross-critique prompts asking models to judge gender fairness and suggest improvements.
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: multiple independent models with self- and cross-evaluation
evidence_records.Agent roles: depression predictor and qualitative fairness critic
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers define prompts/metrics, balance the qualitative subset, and two analysts independently code fairness explanations before jointly finalizing themes.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: interview dialogue and its LLM depression explanation/fairness critique
evidence_records.Generated outputs: PHQ-8 predictions, rationales, fairness critiques, quantitative bias scores, codes and themes
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Themes are illustrated with model-output quotations, but predictions and critiques are not released with a complete sample-level provenance package.
evidence_records.Baselines: three LLMs, three gender-information prompt conditions, benchmark PHQ labels, and self-versus-cross-model critiques
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: not reported; LLaMA/ChatGPT temperature 0.7 and maximum output 200 tokens
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: precision, recall, F1, accuracy, statistical parity, equal opportunity, equalized odds, equal accuracy, word/character count and BERT sentiment
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two researchers independently conduct thematic-analysis phases 1–3 on model critiques and meet to finalize phases 4–6; no external mental-health or fairness expert evaluation is reported.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two study researchers; clinical/fairness qualitative expertise is not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: group-fairness ratios and descriptive means/SDs; word-count and response-length differences are reported significant, while sentiment and outcome differences are not
evidence_records.Principal results: ChatGPT led classification metrics and produced longer, more contextual critiques; LLaMA 2 often led group-fairness ratios but generated shorter, sometimes contradictory critiques. Themes include assumptions, gender-neutral language, desired model traits and improvement suggestions.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: LLaMA 2 required 400 hours on four NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB GPUs; API/runtime costs for other models are not reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The paper focuses centrally on fairness/explainability and uses owner-anonymized data, but does not report a new ethics review, consent for LLM processing, retention controls or clinical-risk governance.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Prompts, procedures and detailed result tables are included; code, the 25-sample output set, seeds and exact proprietary snapshots are not linked.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Only three LLMs, two datasets, a small qualitative sample and gender alone are studied; age/race and other mental-health tasks require future work.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Models judge their own or one another's outputs, fairness themes reflect model rhetoric rather than affected-user judgments, overlapping chunks may overweight context, and no clinician or participant validates depression explanations.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Secondary analysis of established DAIC-WOZ/E-DAIC benchmark families; not an independent data collection.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Adjacent high-stakes evidence for RQ6–RQ8: aggregate accuracy can diverge from fairness/explanation quality, and multi-model self-critique is not a substitute for independent stakeholders or clinical safeguards.

quality_scores.Title: CollabCoder: A Lower-barrier, Rigorous Workflow for Inductive Collaborative Qualitative Analysis with Large Language Models

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: The paper explicitly grounds the three-stage workflow in collaborative qualitative analysis, Grounded Theory, and thematic-analysis practices.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Two 15-review subsets support a controlled usability comparison but are small, artificial, and unlike real sensitive research corpora.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: The system stages, gpt-3.5-turbo role, temperature, prompts, preprocessing, similarity calculations, and interfaces are described in detail.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Atlas.ti Web is a useful independent system comparator, but the design does not isolate every LLM contribution from workflow/interface differences.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: A counterbalanced within-subject study with 16 participants in eight pairs, questionnaires, observations, and interviews directly evaluates the workflow.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Cohen's kappa and semantic-similarity agreement are reported, but the 0.8 threshold and their relation to interpretive quality are not validated.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Independent coding and discussion preserve some plurality, yet the workflow still emphasizes consensus and participants reported possible GPT dominance.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Users can trace codes and decisions to raw data, record keyword supports/certainty, and inspect both coders' contributions.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: No repeated GPT runs, seeds, or robustness analysis is reported.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: The study reports IRB approval, consent for recording, participant compensation, and a non-sensitive public task corpus.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompt templates, public data, model name, and a project page are available, but a fixed model snapshot and complete reproducible run package are not reported.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Conclusions are bounded to workflow support and usability, and the authors explicitly discuss idealized tasks, reliance, and GPT-dominance risks.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: The total is a compact audit aid, not a ranking; interpret every dimension against the paper's claim and study design.

quality_scores.Title: Supporting Serendipity: Opportunities and Challenges for Human-AI Collaboration in Qualitative Analysis

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: The interview, open-coding, iterative category formation, grounded memo, and all-author review process is clearly described.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Seventeen active qualitative researchers provide relevant evidence, but the sample is institution/CSCW-centered and mostly junior.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: No computational system, model, or operational AI workflow is implemented.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: No system baseline or independent computational comparator is evaluated.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: The 17-participant interview study is appropriate for formative requirements, but it does not evaluate actual use of an AI tool.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: No automatic metric is proposed or validated.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: The central analysis treats ambiguity, disagreement, doubt, and serendipity as valuable rather than errors to eliminate.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Theme memos and reported participant quotations visibly ground the interpretive claims in source interviews.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: No repeated analysis, independent recoding, or stability assessment is reported.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: IRB approval, anonymization, demographic non-linkage, and participant compensation are reported.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Interview transcripts, analysis materials, and code are not reported as openly available.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: The authors limit claims to formative implications and explicitly state that no model, algorithm, or deployed system was evaluated.

quality_scores.Title: Prompting as Panacea? A Case Study of In-Context Learning Performance for Qualitative Coding of Classroom Dialog

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: The paper clearly defines fixed-label educational coding tasks but operationalizes qualitative coding as classification rather than an interpretive methodology.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Five established classroom/tutoring datasets spanning nine tasks and roughly 2,500–50,000 examples provide a strong task-specific test bed.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Models, prompt regimes, temperature, fine-tuning procedures, classifiers, hardware, and full prompt templates are reported.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Random, RoBERTa, Mistral-embedding, zero-shot, few-shot, and full-data comparisons provide strong independent baselines.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Existing human labels anchor performance, but no new expert assessment of model rationales or interpretive validity is conducted.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: F1 is suitable for fixed-label classification but is not validated as a measure of qualitative interpretation and lacks uncertainty estimates.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Each instance is treated as having a correct fixed label; alternative interpretations are not evaluated.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: The paper evaluates labels rather than source-grounded explanations or traceable qualitative evidence.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Three demonstration samples test some few-shot variability, but complete repeated-run and prompt-robustness testing is absent.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: The paper identifies API privacy/storage risk and withholds restricted data from GPT-4, but broader dataset consent/governance reporting is limited.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompts, datasets, and model families are documented, while source code and the exact GPT-4 snapshot are not reported.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: The cautious conclusion that fine-tuning remains valuable is supported across tasks, and prompt, cost, privacy, and contamination limits are acknowledged.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: The total is a compact audit aid, not a ranking; interpret every dimension against the paper's claim and study design.

quality_scores.Title: A mixed-methods study comparing human-led and ChatGPT-driven qualitative analysis in medical education research

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: The paper explicitly follows Braun and Clarke's six phases within a stated post-positivist convergent mixed-methods design.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Public interview data and prior analysis are well motivated, but only a small selected portion is processed and its size is not quantified.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Sequential prompts and outputs are supplied, but the GPT-4 snapshot and complete executable workflow are not.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: A prior human analysis provides a meaningful comparator, although its authors/reviewers also evaluate the model and the human score is fixed.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Three highly knowledgeable assessors provide both structured ratings and qualitative comments, followed by an integrated analysis.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: The custom human scales are not automatic metrics and are not independently validated for qualitative quality.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Qualitative comments expose meaningful model-human differences, but the quantitative frame still anchors one human analysis as the reference.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Staged outputs make some data links visible, yet prompt-background contamination shows that source-only provenance is not enforced.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Only one GPT analysis is run and no robustness test is reported.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Use of already-public data and cloud-privacy warnings are reported, while broader governance detail is limited.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Public source material and supplemental prompts/outputs are available, but code and an exact snapshot are absent.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: The conclusions foreground prompt contamination, shallow context, assessor overlap, and the continued need for human theory and verification.
